title: The Performance Artist

jokes.text: Larry introduces George Segal as needing 'no introduction' while simultaneously introducing him
jokes.setup: Larry says 'needs no introduction'
jokes.punchline: He then proceeds to fully introduce him anyway
jokes.explanation: A classic talk-show cliché played straight — the show's meta-satirical lens makes it land as gentle mockery of the genre's hollow conventions. Functional but unremarkable; the joke is on the format itself.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: When does that come out?

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: I don't know.

jokes.text: Larry asks about George Segal's movie 'Me, Myself, and I' featuring JoBeth Williams: 'Is she all three -- me, myself, and I?'
jokes.setup: George mentions JoBeth Williams is in a movie called 'Me, Myself, and I'
jokes.punchline: Larry asks if she's playing all three personalities implied by the title
jokes.explanation: A sharp, economical wordplay joke that works on two levels: the literal absurdity of the question, and Larry's obliviousness/awkwardness as an interviewer. The phrasing is swift and the construction is tidy. It's one of the better quick-fire gags in the opening segment.

dialogue.line: And has she been released?
No. She's still in the can.

jokes.text: Running gag: Every movie George Segal mentions, Larry asks 'When does that come out?' and Segal answers 'I don't know.'
jokes.setup: George lists multiple movies he's completed; Larry dutifully asks each time when they'll be released
jokes.punchline: Each time, George's answer is a flat 'I don't know' — the repetition escalates the absurdity
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured running gag that satirizes the hollow promotional format of late-night interviews. Each repetition compounds the comedy — an actor who has made multiple movies that nobody can see and whose star doesn't even know the release dates. The deadpan delivery earns this. It's earned comedy from a specific, observed truth about the talk show format.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I almost had to run to the can myself

jokes.text: Larry asks why Segal was selling his Beverly Hills house; Segal says 'We were getting out of town.' Larry asks 'And has she been released?' Segal: 'No. She's still in the can.'
jokes.setup: Larry has been using 'in the can' to mean 'completed/filmed'; conversation shifts to personal life and Segal's wife; 'still in the can' now sounds like she's in prison or in a bathroom
jokes.punchline: 'She's still in the can' — the phrase carries double meaning (completed film vs. jail/bathroom), punctuated by Segal's straight delivery
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke of the opening interview. The setup is built gradually and organically through the conversation — 'in the can' has been established as movie-business jargon, then applied to Segal's wife in a way that sounds darkly like she's incarcerated. The double meaning is perfectly planted and pays off with maximum economy. It's the kind of joke that only works because of patient structural setup.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: But we have him on every month, Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Hank's on every night.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I've been meaning to talk to you about that.

jokes.text: Artie riffs backstage on 'in the can': 'When you said that thing about his wife Linda in the can, I split a gut. I almost had to run to the can myself.'
jokes.setup: The 'in the can' joke has just happened on air
jokes.punchline: Artie extends the wordplay one step further by using 'the can' in its bathroom meaning
jokes.explanation: A competent callback that squeezes additional juice from the prior joke, but it's secondary comedy — it can only exist because joke #4 worked. Artie's delivery characteristically extends the gag with his own spin, which is character-consistent. Solid but not independently remarkable.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Ben vereen. Up and tapping, thank god. Susan dey. Pertful little skirtfull.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I've been meaning to talk to you about that.' — responding to Artie's 'Hank's on every night' with a nervous deflection
jokes.setup: Artie has just landed the 'Hank's on every night' zinger
jokes.punchline: Larry's instinctive, cowardly deflection — signaling he knows Artie is right but cannot confront it — is the joke
jokes.explanation: A character-comedy beat that relies entirely on Larry's established spinelessness. The laugh comes from recognition — of course Larry immediately pivots rather than engaging. Strong character integration keeps this above average even though it's not a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That's why the good lord invented videotape.

jokes.text: The network's proposed 'dazzling' fall schedule: Marla Gibbs, Conrad Bain, Ben Vereen ('Up and tapping, thank god'), Susan Dey ('pertful little skirtfull')
jokes.setup: The network sends a memo demanding the show book their 'stars'
jokes.punchline: Artie reads them off with increasingly arch commentary — 'Prepare to be dazzled' followed by a list of clearly faded stars, with his own absurd editorial asides
jokes.explanation: Artie's editorial voice ('pertful little skirtfull,' 'Up and tapping, thank god') is where the comedy lives — it's not the guest list itself but Rip Torn's character filtering it through his sardonic worldview. Period-specific but effective insider satire.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: 10:00 tomorrow!

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That means 10:30?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah. 10:30 sharp.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Susan Dey. Pertful little skirtfull.'
jokes.setup: Artie is reading through the network's guest list.
jokes.punchline: 'Pertful little skirtfull' — a nonsense portmanteau compliment that sounds vaguely lewd but means nothing.
jokes.explanation: A weird, funny coinage that feels like something only Rip Torn's Artie would say. 'Pertful' isn't a word but it perfectly conveys Artie's archaic, vaguely lecherous worldview. Low structure score because it doesn't have a payoff — it's a one-off riff — but it's delightfully odd.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Mark my words, children. Somebody is going down. They started with Jerry. They'll do it again.

jokes.text: When Larry vents that he can't remember what he says to guests, Artie delivers: 'That's why the good Lord invented videotape.'
jokes.setup: Larry spirals into existential crisis about the meaninglessness of his interviews
jokes.punchline: Artie punctures the melodrama with a bluntly practical non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: Artie as deflating pragmatist is a reliable comic engine. The joke works because it refuses to honor Larry's self-pity — a clean, economical shutdown. Not exceptional, but well-executed character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: We didn't introduce R.E.M. as "rem" last week.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, my brave, brave Phil. Always with the jokes and yet so very desperate.

jokes.text: Larry demands a staff meeting 'Tomorrow at 10:30' — Artie: 'That means 10:30?' Larry: 'Yeah. 10:30 sharp.' — an implicit acknowledgment that Larry's '10:00' always means '10:30'
jokes.setup: Larry dramatically calls for a 10:00 AM meeting
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately translates this as 10:30, and Larry confirms without missing a beat — exposing the show's (and Larry's) institutional unreliability
jokes.explanation: A small but well-observed comedy of workplace dysfunction. It implies a whole history of Larry's chronic lateness and the staff's weary accommodation of it, all in two lines. Character-specific and efficiently done.

dialogue.line: If somebody gets fired, it will be me.
No. No, it is. I've been here the shortest time.

jokes.text: Hank in the hallway, ominously: 'Mark my words, children. Somebody is going down. They started with Jerry. They'll do it again.'
jokes.setup: Staff waiting nervously for the mystery meeting
jokes.punchline: Hank inflates the stakes to apocalyptic proportions with self-important gravitas, referencing a past firing as if it were a historical atrocity
jokes.explanation: Perfectly calibrated Hank: the pomposity, the self-dramatization, the vague historical allusion. Tambor's delivery of 'Mark my words, children' is its own performance. The line works because it reveals Hank's character — his need to be the sage elder of a drama that doesn't concern him.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: He'll take antidepressants, and everything will be normal.

jokes.text: Phil predicts: 'Larry will decide nothing works on the show and that everything needs to be changed. He'll take antidepressants, and everything will be normal.'
jokes.setup: Staff speculating who will be fired or what will happen at the meeting
jokes.punchline: Phil cuts through all the panic with a veteran's calm: Larry's 'crises' always resolve the same way — medication and inertia
jokes.explanation: A sharp piece of character comedy that works on multiple levels: it's a burn on Larry's neurotic cycles, it's Phil's dry institutional knowledge, and it perfectly predicts the episode's arc. The antidepressants line is the punchline within the punchline. Highly quotable and reveals the show's cynical-but-affectionate view of its protagonist.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm just getting a haircut.

jokes.text: Hank, immediately after Phil's sensible prediction: 'If someone gets fired, it should be Mike. He's been here the shortest.'
jokes.setup: Phil has just delivered a measured, insightful prediction about how the crisis will resolve
jokes.punchline: Hank ignores all of it and returns to his primary concern — self-preservation through sacrificing someone else — with cheerful sociopathy
jokes.explanation: Hank as cheerful institutional predator. The joke is in the pivot — after genuine insight from Phil, Hank's non-sequitur reduction to 'throw Mike to the wolves' is perfectly in character and darkly funny. His total lack of self-awareness is the engine.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey, a haircut, huh?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No. He's just checking it.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That's a great haircut.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He's just started.

jokes.text: Larry greets the barber in French ('Gustave, ça va. Time for a trim later? Merci.') mid-staff-crisis, implying this is normal behavior for him
jokes.setup: Larry is supposedly rushing everyone into the urgent meeting
jokes.punchline: He pauses to schmooze his barber in affected French, revealing his vanity is prioritized over the crisis he himself called
jokes.explanation: A visual/behavioral character beat that works by contrast — the urgent meeting leader stopped cold by his own vanity. Good character integration, lightly funny in context.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Do you want to just give me one second?

jokes.text: Hank complimenting the barber's work before it's started: 'That's a great haircut.' Staff member: 'He's just started.' Hank: 'I can tell that will be a great one.'
jokes.setup: Hank sees Larry's barber just beginning the haircut
jokes.punchline: Hank reflexively compliments something that doesn't exist yet — pure sycophancy operating on autopilot
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean Hank joke — his fawning is so automatic it fires before he has any information to fawn about. Efficient and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I can sum up with one word-- guests.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Guests. Thank you, Jesus.
What did you think the problem was?
[All] Guests.

jokes.text: Larry's dramatic meeting setup trails into an awkward 30-second silence before he can articulate the problem
jokes.setup: Larry has called an emergency meeting with great urgency and told everyone there is 'a serious problem here at the show'
jokes.punchline: He then visibly struggles to remember or articulate what the problem is, producing a long, painful pause
jokes.explanation: A prototypical Larry Sanders Show cringe beat — the man who called the meeting cannot lead it. The pause deflates all his dramatic posturing. In a no-laugh-track single-camera show, this kind of silence is weaponized. Gains rewatch value because on rewatch you see it coming and dread it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I know you, Kiki. How's your... How's your, uh--

dialogue.speaker: Kiki
dialogue.line: Well. Thanks.

jokes.text: Larry finally reduces the 'serious problem' to one word: 'Guests.' Staff member whispers: 'Thank you, Jesus.'
jokes.setup: Larry has built up enormous suspense with his halting, ominous preamble about 'a serious problem'
jokes.punchline: The 'one-word' summation is 'Guests' — an entirely mundane booking issue — and a staff member's muttered 'Thank you, Jesus' punctuates the collective relief/deflation
jokes.explanation: Classic anticlimax structure: build the tension to a breaking point, deliver the most underwhelming possible reveal. The 'Thank you, Jesus' reaction punctuates it perfectly without overselling. Well-crafted deflation.

dialogue.line: Could you repeat that last part?
Which part?
About the people...
Was I unclear about--
Clear to me.
Perfectly clear.

jokes.text: Larry asks 'What did you think the problem was?' — the entire staff simultaneously answers 'Guests.'
jokes.setup: Larry is fishing for validation that his problem identification was insightful
jokes.punchline: The whole staff answers in unison that they already knew — they were just waiting for Larry to catch up to what they all knew
jokes.explanation: A quick follow-up beat that doubles down on the deflation — Larry's 'revelation' was already obvious to everyone. The unison response is a crisp comedic payoff. Slightly less powerful than the preceding setup because it's an afterthought, but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Could you repeat that last part?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Which part?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: About the people...

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Was I unclear about--

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Clear to me. Perfectly clear.

jokes.text: Larry addresses the booking coordinator by name ('Great, thank you... Kiki. Kiki. I know you, Kiki. How's your... how's your, uh— Well. Thanks.')
jokes.setup: Larry tries to show he's a 'people person' by addressing a staff member by name
jokes.punchline: He can't remember anything about her beyond her name, fumbles a personal question into nothing, and pivots awkwardly
jokes.explanation: A perfect cringe beat. The whole scene is predicated on Larry trying to project engaged leadership, and this moment exposes that he literally doesn't know his own staff. The trailing off into 'Well. Thanks.' is painfully real. Strong character integration — this could only be Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And who is Al Nelson?
He's the plate spinner.
He was a regular on Sullivan 30 years ago.

jokes.text: Larry tells staff to find guests 'other talk shows haven't gotten.' Someone immediately asks him to repeat it. He does, clearly perplexed it wasn't understood. Multiple people confirm it was perfectly clear.
jokes.setup: Larry delivers his grand insight about booking unique guests
jokes.punchline: Someone asks him to repeat the last part — implying either confusion or (more likely) disbelief that this is the master strategy — Larry re-states it with mounting confusion, while others rush to validate him
jokes.explanation: Another cringe beat about the sycophancy surrounding Larry — his banal insight treated as proclamation, with staff both gently challenging and then immediately validating it. Competent character work but slightly diffuse.

dialogue.line: He's older now, and he's started using Chinette, but people still flip for him.

jokes.text: Larry challenges the booking of Tony Randall ('Tony's on what? Every other week?'), then Jay Thomas ('Who is Jay Thomas?'), then Al Nelson the plate spinner ('He was a regular on Sullivan 30 years ago... He's older now and he's started using Chinette, but people still flip for him.')
jokes.setup: Larry reviews the current week's guest list looking for the problem
jokes.punchline: The list escalates in obscurity and datedness, culminating in Artie's description of the plate spinner now using paper plates — a brilliantly specific absurd detail
jokes.explanation: The 'Chinette' line is the gem here — a tiny, specific, absurd detail (the vaudeville plate spinner has downgraded to disposable plates) that perfectly embodies the show's satire of TV's recycled entertainment culture. Escalating structure works well; the payoff is specific enough to feel earned and original.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: This is a booking problem, right?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Phil, shut the fuck up.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'll handle it. Phil, shut the fuck up.

jokes.text: Phil cautiously asks to clarify: 'Just so I'm clear about this, this is a booking problem, right?' Artie: 'Phil, shut the fuck up.' Then Larry: 'Phil, shut the fuck up.'
jokes.setup: Phil tries to reduce the mounting anxiety to a simple question
jokes.punchline: Both Artie and Larry immediately fire the same dismissal at him in sequence, as if by reflex — the authority figures instinctively silencing the voice of reason
jokes.explanation: The double dismissal — both Artie and Larry independently telling Phil to shut up — has a perfect comedic rhythm. The institutional suppression of the sensible voice is both funny and a pointed comment on the show's power dynamics. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Mike, you're new here.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I'll let that slide, but--

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank, put your hand down.

jokes.text: Staff brainstorming 'new' guests — Hank immediately suggests Robert Conrad ('Owes me a favor. Pick up the phone. Hello, Bobby.')
jokes.setup: Larry has just finished demanding fresh, new faces — no more same old guests
jokes.punchline: Hank's first contribution is to call in a personal favor with an aged TV star he knows, completely missing the point of what 'new' means
jokes.explanation: Classic Hank — he hears 'do something' and interprets it as 'do something for me personally.' The name-dropping of a favor with Robert Conrad is perfectly in character, and Larry's flat 'That's not what we're looking for' punctuates it efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Robert Conrad.
No. No. Owes me a favor. Pick up the phone. Hello, Bobby.

jokes.text: Artie's contribution to 'new' guests: 'Ho! Raymond Burr, with whom I once had the honor of playing golf. He's in the new Perry Mason show. Hello, Perry.'
jokes.setup: Staff is supposed to be brainstorming genuinely fresh, new talent
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'new' suggestion is Raymond Burr — a man in his 70s reprising a role from the 1950s — delivered with complete sincerity and a golf anecdote
jokes.explanation: A companion joke to Hank's misfires — now Artie, the supposed adult in the room, is equally guilty of suggesting 'new' guests from the Eisenhower era. The golf anecdote is a characteristically Artie touch — name-dropping as social currency even in a staff meeting.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Raymond Burr, with whom I once had the honor of playing golf.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hello, Perry.

jokes.text: Paula pitches Tim Miller; Hank responds: 'Performance art. That's a bunch of dog poop. What does he do? Get stark naked? Cover himself with chocolate syrup?'
jokes.setup: A booker suggests a provocative performance artist as the 'new' guest Larry wants
jokes.punchline: Hank's immediate, confident characterization of all performance art as 'dog poop' followed by his specific mental image of what it involves — which is accidentally not far off
jokes.explanation: Hank's cultural philistinism is perfectly calibrated — 'dog poop' as cultural criticism is funny precisely because it's so reductive. His guesses about naked bodies and chocolate syrup are funnier because performance art does sometimes involve those things, making his dismissal weirdly informed.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Performance art. That's a bunch of dog poop. What does he do? Get stark naked? Cover himself with chocolate syrup?

jokes.text: Paula reads from Tim Miller's review: 'A garrulous assault of anecdote, humor, observation, and social comment punctuated by movement and channeled through life experience.' Larry: 'Good. Book him.'
jokes.setup: Larry has asked 'Is he funny?' — a reasonable question; Paula reads an impenetrable critical description
jokes.punchline: Larry hears the word-salad description and immediately says 'Good. Book him' — either he's pretending to understand or he's simply given up trying and defaulted to credentializing language
jokes.explanation: A sharp satirical beat about how critical language substitutes for actual judgment. Larry can't parse the review but the vocabulary sounds impressive, so he books the act. This is insider media satire at its most efficient.

dialogue.line: Reading the pretentious review: 'A garrulous assault of anecdote, humor, observation, and social comment punctuated by movement and channeled through life experience.'

jokes.text: Tim Miller's performance: 'Suddenly I'm thrown out of my father's penis into my mom's body. I'm surrounded by thousands of squirming creatures. I'm swimming upstream — one queer spermlette fighting the odds.'
jokes.setup: Tim Miller performs his piece on Larry's talk show to a live audience.
jokes.punchline: 'One queer spermlette fighting the odds' — the origin story reframed as a gay liberation narrative at the cellular level.
jokes.explanation: This is genuinely creative writing — using conception as a political metaphor for queer identity. 'Spermlette' is a delightful coinage. The piece is more performance art than stand-up, but it's inherently comedic in its absurdist framing. Tagged as standup/performance since it's a staged piece within the show-within-the-show.

dialogue.line: A sperm looking like Jesse Helms tries to catch me. I elude him and find a willing lesbian ovum.

jokes.text: Tim Miller's performance piece: 'Suddenly I'm thrown out of my father's penis into my mom's body... I'm one queer spermlette fighting the odds. A sperm looking like Jesse Helms tries to catch me. I elude him and find a willing lesbian ovum. We fertilize... Ecce homo. Behold the fag.'
jokes.setup: A 'very provocative monologist' has been booked to represent fresh, edgy content on the show
jokes.punchline: The performance is genuinely avant-garde — mixing birth metaphor, queer identity, political imagery (Jesse Helms as predatory sperm), and Latin proclamation — performed live to a confused talk-show audience
jokes.explanation: The performance art piece is genuinely original and daring for a 1993 network context — it's not meant to be a conventional joke but it IS comedic in its specificity and audacity. The Jesse Helms-as-sperm image is memorably transgressive. The gap between the piece's earnestness and the audience's confusion IS the comedy. Scores high on originality because this specific conceit is genuinely unusual even by today's standards.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: All right. All right. That is not necessary.

jokes.text: Tim Miller: 'A sperm looking like Jesse Helms tries to catch me. I elude him and find a willing lesbian ovum. We fertilize. There's an explosion of creative electricity.'
jokes.setup: Tim Miller's sperm-narrative origin story continues.
jokes.punchline: Jesse Helms as the antagonist sperm; the lesbian ovum as the cooperative partner — a miniature gay rights allegory at the cellular level.
jokes.explanation: Jesse Helms as a 'hideous sperm' is audaciously specific political comedy. The image is genuinely outrageous and funny — casting the era's most prominent anti-gay politician as the villain in a conception allegory is sharp and original. The 'willing lesbian ovum' and 'power-share' are clever continuations of the metaphor.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I apologize for our audience. Let's try and stay open.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Right. Stay open.

jokes.text: Audience boos Tim Miller; Larry desperately: 'All right. All right. That is not necessary.' An audience member shouts 'Go back to San Francisco!' Miller: 'I'm from L.A.'
jokes.setup: The performance piece has ended with light applause and then growing audience hostility
jokes.punchline: The audience member's geographically illiterate heckle ('Go back to San Francisco!') is punctured by Miller's flat factual correction
jokes.explanation: Economically devastating. The heckle contains its own prejudice (equating gay = San Francisco), and Miller's deadpan geographic correction is the perfect response — refusing to engage with the homophobia while clinically correcting the factual error. Maximum economy, very funny, and socially pointed without being didactic.

dialogue.speaker: Audience member
dialogue.line: Go back to San Francisco!

dialogue.speaker: Tim Miller
dialogue.line: I'm from L.A.

jokes.text: [Man from audience]: 'Go back to San Francisco!' / Tim Miller: 'I'm from L.A.'
jokes.setup: An audience member heckles Tim Miller with the classic homophobic dismissal 'Go back to San Francisco.'
jokes.punchline: Tim's flat correction — 'I'm from L.A.' — deflates the heckle without even engaging with its intent.
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum comedy. The heckler's 'Go back to San Francisco' is a cliché homophobic jeer — Tim doesn't dignify it with a political response, just a geographic correction. The joke is beautiful in its economy and confidence: Tim doesn't need to win the argument because the heckler's premise is factually wrong at the most basic level. This is deadpan perfection and one of the episode's most quotable moments.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I warned you with my eyes.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I heard nothing. I saw nothing.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I warned you with my eyes.' Larry: 'I heard nothing. I saw nothing.'
jokes.setup: Artie claims he warned Larry about the content
jokes.punchline: Artie's claim to have 'warned with his eyes' is both plausible (very Artie) and absurd; Larry's 'I heard nothing, I saw nothing' is a Sergeant Schultz-style complete denial
jokes.explanation: Both parts of the exchange work: Artie's eye-warning as a legit communication method, and Larry's flat denial. Good rhythm and character-specific — Larry's cowardice rendered in three words.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The tape was not that gay.

jokes.text: Larry: 'The tape was not that gay.' Artie: 'I don't mind the gay thing. He's talking about butt plugs. He's talking about his father's orgasm.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie try to articulate exactly what they object to
jokes.punchline: Larry's complaint is 'too gay'; Artie, who usually plays enforcer, clarifies it's not the gayness but the extremely specific sexual content — 'butt plugs' and 'his father's orgasm' — listed with increasing gravity
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: it exposes Larry's implicit homophobia (his objection is 'too gay') while Artie inadvertently provides the more damning specific inventory. 'His father's orgasm' said with Artie's deadpan gravity is genuinely funny. Good character differentiation between Larry's vagueness and Artie's horrifying specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He's talking about butt plugs. He's talking about his father's orgasm.

jokes.text: Artie tells Tim Miller: 'We think you're terrific, timbo. The network simply will not let us air it.' — an outright lie delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.setup: The show has decided to pull Miller's segment; they need to explain this to him
jokes.punchline: Artie blames 'the network' with total conviction — classic institutional buck-passing — while the audience knows it was entirely their own decision
jokes.explanation: Corporate cowardice played to perfection. Artie's sincerity while lying is excellent character comedy — he's not embarrassed, he's professionally fluent in this kind of misdirection. The audience's knowledge that it's a lie gives it dramatic irony.

jokes.text: The moment Miller is gone, Larry: 'You think he bought the network thing?' Artie: 'Entirely.' Larry: 'We're not completely lying. We can't air this, right?'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie have just finished a convincing performance of indignation at network censorship
jokes.punchline: They immediately drop the act entirely — Larry's 'we're not completely lying' is a perfect piece of moral gymnastics, the smallest possible fig leaf of self-justification
jokes.explanation: Larry's 'we're not completely lying' is a beautiful rationalization — it reveals his need to maintain a self-image of honesty even while blatantly lying. This is strong character writing because it's psychologically specific to Larry's particular brand of cowardice.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Listen to me, Melody, the man said "butt plug" three times! And you and I both know you can't--
You can say "butt plug"? Since when?

jokes.text: Artie on the phone with the network: 'Listen to me, Melody, the man said 'butt plug' three times! And you and I both know you can't— You can say 'butt plug'? Since when?'
jokes.setup: Artie is calling the network to get them to officially object to the Miller segment so they can legitimize the censorship
jokes.punchline: The network informs him 'butt plug' is apparently permissible on HBO — revealing that Artie (and Larry) are more prudish than the network they blamed, and their moral line is arbitrary
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The reveal that 'butt plug' is permissible on their own network completely destroys the position Larry and Artie have just defended — they're more conservative than the network they blamed. Artie's stunned 'Since when?' perfectly captures the comedy of a man who has just been outflanked by permissiveness. Excellent structure, strong character integration (Artie's outrage at being told he was WRONG about what's unacceptable), and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The network says that it is our decision and they find no problem with the piece.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: They're hanging us out to dry.

jokes.text: Artie hangs up and announces: 'Good news? The network says that it is our decision and they find no problem with the piece.' Then: 'They're hanging us out to dry.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie were counting on the network to provide cover for their censorship decision
jokes.punchline: The 'good news' framing followed immediately by the real meaning — the network has refused to share the blame — is a classic Artie reversal
jokes.explanation: The ironic framing of 'Good news?' for genuinely bad news is a clean structural joke. The network has beaten them at their own game of institutional buck-passing. Satisfying ironic reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You can say 'butt plug'? Since when?

jokes.text: Larry: 'I don't want to be part of cutting him.' Artie: 'Well, you want me to make the decision?' Larry: 'I'd like to participate in some limited capacity.'
jokes.setup: Larry is faced with making an uncomfortable decision about whether to air Miller's segment
jokes.punchline: 'I'd like to participate in some limited capacity' — Larry wants to be involved in the decision-making to the minimum possible degree, essentially asking Artie to decide while giving him nominal credit
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's crown jewels. 'I'd like to participate in some limited capacity' is precisely the kind of corporate-speak that perfectly encodes Larry's pathological conflict-avoidance. It sounds like something from a HR manual deployed to describe a man who wants credit without responsibility. The character integration is near-perfect — this sentence could ONLY be said by Larry Sanders. Highly quotable, psychologically precise, economical. Justifies 8+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'll count to 10, and if you agree with my choice, don't say anything.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I agree.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Then don't say anything.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I got excited. I had the answer.

jokes.text: Artie proposes to count to 10, and if Larry doesn't say anything, he agrees with the decision to cut Miller. Larry: '1, 2, 3, 4—' Larry: 'I agree.' Artie: 'Then don't say anything.' Larry: 'I got excited. I had the answer.'
jokes.setup: Artie has devised a system where Larry can avoid directly deciding by staying silent
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately breaks the system by enthusiastically announcing his agreement before the count is done, and then explaining he got 'excited' about having the answer — the man cannot even be passive correctly
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. The setup is already funny (Artie has to invent a system to let Larry do nothing), and the punchline is brilliant — Larry sabotages even his own passivity. He was supposed to say NOTHING and instead jumped in with the answer before being asked, then explains he got excited because he 'had the answer.' This is a perfect encapsulation of Larry's paradox: simultaneously conflict-avoidant and approval-seeking. The structure is flawless — the absurdist silence-as-agreement system, the premature break, the delightfully human excuse. Comparable in quality to the 8.0+ benchmark anchors; the structure and character integration here are exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I agree.
Then don't say anything.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I got excited. I had the answer.

jokes.text: Phil tells the staff he told his friends to watch Tim Miller last night because 'they haven't seen anything that good since my college roommate's nervous breakdown.'
jokes.setup: Phil is sharing his enthusiasm for Tim Miller's performance
jokes.punchline: The comparison — great art vs. someone's actual mental collapse — is darkly funny in its implied equivalence, and the specificity ('college roommate') makes it feel real
jokes.explanation: A beautifully dark and economical line. Phil's genuine enthusiasm for Miller's work, expressed through the most damning comparison possible, is a great piece of comedy writing. 'Nervous breakdown' as a compliment carries real wit. Highly quotable and distinctly Phil.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I told my friends to watch Tim Miller last night.
Why, Phil?

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: They haven't seen anything that good since my college roommate's nervous breakdown.

jokes.text: Artie reads Liz Smith's column: 'Sanders cans performance by Miller. Late-night funny man Larry Sanders couldn't take the heat last night, so he threw Mr. Miller out of the kitchen.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just made the 'private' decision to cut Miller, blaming the network
jokes.punchline: Liz Smith's column has correctly identified Larry as solely responsible — the lie has been publicly fact-checked the next morning
jokes.explanation: The irony lands because of the dramatic irony — we watched them construct the lie, and now the press has seen through it. The 'couldn't take the heat / threw him out of the kitchen' is a serviceable mixed metaphor that works as fake gossip-column prose.

dialogue.line: Liz Smith review: 'Sanders cans performance by Miller. Late-night funny man Larry Sanders couldn't take the heat last night, so he threw Mr. Miller out of the kitchen.'

jokes.text: Army Archerd's column: 'Network officials claimed no responsibility for Mr. Miller's unkind cut, saying they had no involvement in the decision.' Larry: 'Rat bastards!'
jokes.setup: Larry blamed the network; the network has now publicly denied all responsibility
jokes.punchline: Larry's outraged 'Rat bastards!' — indignant that the people he tried to blame have refused to take the blame — exposes that his outrage is entirely self-serving
jokes.explanation: 'Rat bastards!' as the response to being accurately quoted is a terrific Larry moment — his moral indignation is entirely misplaced and entirely self-interested. The escalating public humiliation in the newspaper column sequence is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.line: Calling him the Jesse Helms of late-night television.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, hell. That's not so bad.

jokes.text: Artie reads the kicker: Miller called Larry 'the Jesse Helms of late-night television.' Larry: 'Well, hell. That's not so bad.'
jokes.setup: The newspaper humiliation has been escalating; this is the final kicker — Miller has publicly compared Larry to the most notorious anti-gay senator
jokes.punchline: Larry's reaction: 'That's not so bad' — either he doesn't know who Jesse Helms is, or his ego is so fragile that being named at all feels like a win
jokes.explanation: Outstanding character comedy. The callback to Miller's piece (where Jesse Helms was the predatory anti-gay sperm) makes this line even richer on rewatch. Larry either misses the insult entirely or values the mention over its content. 'Well, hell. That's not so bad' — the flatness of delivery and the utter wrongness of the sentiment make this one of the episode's standout moments. Economy is near-perfect. Justifies 8+ because the line encapsulates Larry's narcissism and obliviousness in four words.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm not mentioned in either article.

jokes.text: Hank, reading the same articles: 'How do you think I feel? I'm not mentioned in either article.'
jokes.setup: Larry is humiliated by the negative press; everyone is focused on the crisis
jokes.punchline: Hank's complaint is that he was EXCLUDED from the controversy — he wants to be part of the scandal, just to be mentioned
jokes.explanation: The episode's most purely Hank joke, and one of its best. 'I'm not mentioned in either article' as a COMPLAINT during a PR crisis is a perfect articulation of Hank's bottomless need for attention. He would rather be vilified than irrelevant. This is world-class character writing — specific, unexpected, revealing, and devastating. Economy is exceptional; the joke lands in one sentence with no setup needed. Easily justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Your brain doesn't have any cognizance of anything.

jokes.text: Hank, apparently sitting silently in the corner unnoticed: 'Sorry, boss. We didn't know you were here.' Larry: 'See? You start reading that shit, your brain doesn't have any cognizance of anything.'
jokes.setup: Larry has been ranting and spiraling about the press coverage
jokes.punchline: A revelation: Hank has apparently been in the room the entire time, unnoticed — and Larry's response is to blame the newspapers for his own inattentiveness
jokes.explanation: A mild physical/situational joke — Hank has been in the room the whole time without anyone noticing, which is itself a joke about Hank's irrelevance. Larry's pseudo-philosophical explanation ('cognizance of anything') is characteristic self-justifying nonsense. Good as a contextual beat, not exceptional on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And my, uh, whole face. It looks great.

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: Your whole face.

jokes.text: Artie pivots to a new talk show guest segment: 'We can talk about the surgery. Your plastic surgery is great. You've openly talked about it.' 'Yes, I had my nose done.' 'And your eyes.' 'And my... any cheekbones?' 'And my, uh, whole face.'
jokes.setup: To move past the Miller scandal, they segue into a plastic surgery conversation with a new guest
jokes.punchline: What starts as nose and eyes escalates via Artie's prompting ('Any cheekbones?') to 'my whole face' — suggesting the guest has had so much work done they've effectively replaced their entire face
jokes.explanation: A competent escalation joke about Hollywood plastic surgery excess. Artie's 'Any cheekbones?' is a nice prompt that helps the confession escalate. 'My whole face' as the admission is funny but not especially sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Guest comedian
dialogue.line: If you're so square, I might as well do Leno.

dialogue.speaker: Audience
dialogue.line: Ooh!

jokes.text: Tom Arnold confronts Larry on air about the Miller censorship: 'If you're so square, I might as well do Leno.' Audience: 'Ooh!'
jokes.setup: Tom Arnold is supposed to be doing a friendly guest interview; instead he uses his platform to call Larry out for the censorship
jokes.punchline: 'I might as well do Leno' — invoking Leno as the ultimate epithet for safe, corporate, toothless television — and the audience's collective 'Ooh!' treats it like a genuine insult
jokes.explanation: A pointed industry joke — using Leno as a synecdoche for corporate comedy cowardice works perfectly in 1993 late-night context. The audience 'Ooh!' is a great reaction beat because it confirms the insult landed. Very quotable and media-savvy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I hide them behind a desk.

jokes.text: Tom Arnold invokes Mitzi Shore messing with Larry at the Comedy Store as a parallel to Larry now doing the same to Tim Miller
jokes.setup: Tom is building the case that Larry has become the industry gatekeeper he once suffered under
jokes.punchline: The comparison lands as a sharp structural irony — Larry's own suppression history is deployed against him to expose his hypocrisy
jokes.explanation: A strong thematic argument made through comedy — the show-within-a-show moment where the guest indicts the host using his own history. Works best for viewers familiar with Larry's (or Garry Shandling's) backstory. The point is sharp even without that context.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Miller
dialogue.line: And don't call me Timbo anymore, okay?

jokes.text: Larry, trying to defuse the ambush: 'We'll have him back again. It was just one of those things.' Tom: 'I thought you had more balls than that.' Larry: 'Wait a minute. No, no. I got to speak now. Speaking as a man who thinks— I know this man.'
jokes.setup: Larry is being publicly cornered into defending his decision by Tom Arnold on his own show
jokes.punchline: Larry's attempted comeback — 'Speaking as a man who thinks' — trails off before a thought is formed; he abandons the sentence and pivots to a non-argument ('I know this man') — publicly demonstrating exactly the lack of balls Tom accused him of
jokes.explanation: Larry publicly proving the accusation while trying to disprove it is a beautiful cringe construction. 'Speaking as a man who thinks' is a perfect incomplete thought — it captures his panic. The verbal disintegration under pressure is peak Larry and near-perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Miller
dialogue.line: Television degrades everybody on it and everybody who watches it.

jokes.text: Artie interjects to defend Larry: 'I have to interject. Uh, he has balls. I got to say it.' Larry: 'I have balls. But they're little, tiny ones. I hide them behind a desk.'
jokes.setup: Tom Arnold has accused Larry of lacking courage; Artie tries to defend him
jokes.punchline: Larry agrees with his own defense ('I have balls') then immediately undermines it with the specific qualification: they're 'little, tiny ones' that he hides behind his desk
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's signature joke and one of its finest moments of writing. Larry starts to defend himself ('I have balls'), then in a single breath transforms it into the most complete self-deprecating capitulation imaginable: 'little, tiny ones' that he 'hides behind a desk.' The admission is simultaneously deeply honest, self-aware, and cowardly — he knows exactly who he is, and that knowledge changes nothing. The character integration is extraordinary — this could only be Larry Sanders. The desk as the literal hiding place for his metaphorical courage is a perfect visual-comic image. Audience applause confirms the reaction. Fully justifies 8+, approaches the 9.5 anchor in character specificity and quotability.

jokes.text: Tom Arnold asking about the Miller situation: 'Because it was gay material.' Larry: 'No. That has nothing to do with it.' The entire conversation then reveals it was entirely about the gay content.
jokes.setup: Larry denies the censorship was about homophobia
jokes.punchline: The denial itself is transparently false — the whole episode has shown it was entirely about the gay/sexual content — making Larry's denial the joke
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is strong (the audience knows) but the exchange itself doesn't have great comedic construction — it's more of a thematic point than a joke. Functional but not its best moment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Turn it off. You know, Tim's great. He's got a story to tell. He's telling how we screwed him.

jokes.text: Artie to Miller: 'Mr. Sanders would like to make amends, timbo. It must make you feel quite special.' Miller: 'Yeah, I'm all fucking aglow.'
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to facilitate a rapprochement between Larry and Miller
jokes.punchline: Miller's 'I'm all fucking aglow' is a perfectly calibrated sarcastic response to Artie's oleaginous diplomacy
jokes.explanation: 'I'm all fucking aglow' is a great line — the formality of 'aglow' against the vulgarity of the f-word and the withering sarcasm makes it pop. Clean, economical, and character-specific to someone who uses language precisely.

dialogue.speaker: Guest
dialogue.line: There's this comic I saw on the Leno show-- a guy named Tim Miller-- who would have been sensational. He's the kind of guy who'd be perfect on this show. You should book him.

jokes.text: Miller to Artie: 'And don't call me Timbo anymore, okay?' Artie: 'Oh, quite right. That's inexcusable. May I call you Tim?' Miller: 'Yeah.' Artie: 'Is that yes?'
jokes.setup: Miller corrects Artie's diminutive nickname
jokes.punchline: Artie performs exaggerated contrition ('That's inexcusable') then immediately asks 'Is that yes?' to a perfectly clear 'Yeah' — either a power move or a hearing issue, both funny
jokes.explanation: A small, well-executed Artie beat — his mock formality and the 'Is that yes?' suggest he's either hard of hearing or asserting control through faux-precision. Character-consistent and mildly amusing.

jokes.text: Miller to Larry and Artie: 'You're just puppets. I just won't appeal to the lowest common denominator, ok? Television degrades everybody on it and everybody who watches it. Now, Tim. Fuck it, and fuck television. I don't need it.'
jokes.setup: Larry has asked Miller to come back and do something 'we can air'
jokes.punchline: Miller refuses with a full philosophical denunciation of television — while ON television — then apparently begins performing his piece again in their office
jokes.explanation: 'Television degrades everybody on it and everybody who watches it' — while being on television — is a sharp irony. Miller's righteous denunciation followed by him immediately launching into his piece anyway gives the scene an absurd quality.

jokes.text: Miller begins performing his piece again spontaneously in the hallway/office: 'A hideous sperm that looks like Senator Jesse Helms—' then completes the full piece again
jokes.setup: Miller has just said 'Fuck television, I don't need it' and seems to be storming out
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots into performing his banned performance piece again — the man who doesn't need television performs for an audience of two executives
jokes.explanation: The structural irony of Miller performing the anti-TV piece for TV executives immediately after his anti-TV speech is pointed and funny. The callback to the original performance hits differently because of the changed context. Good absurdist energy.

jokes.text: Tim Miller does an interview on another show about Larry censoring him; the interviewer says 'I can't believe that's the same piece of material they wouldn't let you do on Larry Sanders' show.'
jokes.setup: Larry is watching Miller on another show
jokes.punchline: The piece Miller performed privately is now being celebrated on a rival show — the censorship has created exactly the publicity and sympathy it was supposed to avoid
jokes.explanation: A structurally satisfying ironic reversal — the Streisand Effect in action, before the term existed. The joke is at Larry's expense and confirms Phil's earlier point about the show's institutional cowardice. Well-constructed karmic payoff.

jokes.text: The rival talk show host tells Miller about America being a 'free country' while clearly performing the same function as Larry's show; Larry watches and says 'Turn it off.'
jokes.setup: The rival host is lecturing about freedom of expression — the same argument Larry made on air
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Turn it off' — he cannot bear watching someone else be the defender of free expression he failed to be
jokes.explanation: 'Turn it off' is a perfect two-word character beat. Larry's inability to watch his own failure celebrated by a competitor is psychologically spot-on. The economy is excellent — we don't need more.

jokes.text: Artie, having watched the whole Miller disaster unfold: 'I finally found the boundaries, huh? This one's in the pocket.'
jokes.setup: The episode has just concluded with Miller getting a better showcase on a rival show, the press coverage humiliating Larry, and the whole thing being a disaster
jokes.punchline: Artie characterizes it all as a productive research exercise — 'I finally found the boundaries' — as if orchestrating a PR disaster was a successful experiment
jokes.explanation: Artie reframing failure as intelligence-gathering is a great character moment — it captures his unflappable ability to find the silver lining in any catastrophe, which is both a survival skill and a form of institutional delusion.

jokes.text: The next in-show guest conversation: 'You're not smoking, which I thought was a delight for you.' Guest: 'It was, but as I say, it's just kind of fallen away.' Larry: 'All right. Just the cigars, I hope.' 'Just the cigars.' 'Everything else is right there.' 'Good. You got to have something to light.'
jokes.setup: Larry comments on the guest having quit smoking
jokes.punchline: 'You got to have something to light' — an oblique joke implying the cigars serve as matches/lighters for other activities, or simply a comically elliptical non-sequitur about needing fire for... something
jokes.explanation: A functional but unremarkable exchange. 'You got to have something to light' lands as mild wordplay but doesn't have much substance. Competent talk show banter played for mild amusement.

jokes.text: Gene Barry mentions Dom DeLuise is in Burke's Law; Larry: 'I'm a big fan of Dom DeLuise.' Gene: 'I am too, but you haven't read the script.'
jokes.setup: Gene Barry is listing the cast of his new show with increasing enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: 'I am too, but you haven't read the script' — a perfectly timed qualification that implies the script is so bad even Dom DeLuise can't save it
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed setup/punchline. The enthusiasm builds with each cast name ('Angie Dickinson... Gerald McRaney... Dom DeLuise' — applause!), and then Gene immediately undercuts his own pitch with devastating economy. 'I am too, but you haven't read the script' is a great line — it simultaneously validates the question and destroys the premise. Excellent structure and economy.

jokes.text: Gene Barry says he saw Tim Miller on the Leno show and recommends Larry book him: 'He's the kind of guy who'd be perfect on this show. You should book him.'
jokes.setup: The episode has resolved with Larry having censored and humiliated Miller
jokes.punchline: The final joke: the most conventional guest on the show — promoting a CBS revival — has seen Miller on Leno and recommends him to Larry, completing the irony of Larry being the last person in television to embrace him
jokes.explanation: A beautiful closing irony: the final guest, representing everything conventional about television (Burke's Law revival, Conrad Bain-era network TV), has discovered Tim Miller on Leno and enthusiastically recommends him to Larry. The circle closes: Larry, who ran from the edgy artist, is now being advised to book him by the squarest possible guest. Strong structural payoff for the whole episode, and the Leno callback makes it richer.

tmdb_overview: In an effort to freshen up the guest list, Larry agrees to have a controversial performance on, then chickens out when he sees the guy's routine.
